children.value: Condensed matter physics is fundamentally concerned with systems containing a very large number of interacting degrees of freedom.
How can simple microscopic components give rise to collective behavior that is qualitatively different from the behavior of the individual components?

children.html: Emergence: collective behavior that cannot be understood from individual components alone\boxed{ \text{Emergence: collective behavior that cannot be understood from individual components alone} }Emergence: collective behavior that cannot be understood from individual components alone​

children.value: The important point is not simply that a many-body system contains many particles. The important point is that increasing the number of degrees of freedom can change the qualitative structure of the problem.
A single atom has discrete energy levels. A macroscopic collection of atoms can form a metal with arbitrarily low-energy excitations.
A single random variable may have almost any probability distribution. The sum of a large number of independent random variables is described by an approximately universal Gaussian distribution.
These are two simple examples of a recurring theme:

children.html: Many≠simply a larger version of one.\boxed{ \text{Many} \neq \text{simply a larger version of one.} }Many=simply a larger version of one.​

4. When does this produce a metal?

children.label: 4. When does this produce a metal?

children.value: We should make one important distinction.
A continuous band does not automatically imply metallic behavior.
Suppose the band is completely filled, and the next band is separated by a finite gap,

children.html: Δband>0.\Delta_{\mathrm{band}}>0.Δband​>0.

children.value: Then the system can still be insulating.
For a metal, the chemical potential lies inside a partially filled band.
Near the Fermi energy, there are occupied and unoccupied states whose energy separation becomes arbitrarily small:

children.html: ΔE∼1N.\Delta E\sim \frac{1}{N}.ΔE∼N1​.
Δexcitation→0(N→∞).\boxed{ \Delta_{\mathrm{excitation}} \rightarrow0 \qquad (N\rightarrow\infty). }Δexcitation​→0(N→∞).​

children.value: The metal therefore possesses low-energy excitations that an isolated atom does not possess.
The collective organization of microscopic states can create entirely new low-energy physics.

6. What did we learn from the atom-to-metal example?

children.label: 6. What did we learn from the atom-to-metal example?

children.value: The microscopic Hamiltonian contains ordinary atoms and ordinary hopping amplitudes.
Nothing singular happens to the microscopic interaction scale.
Nevertheless, simply increasing the number of components produces a qualitatively new structure:

children.html: finite microscopic energy scale+many states⇒arbitrarily small collective energy scales\boxed{ \text{finite microscopic energy scale} + \text{many states} \Rightarrow \text{arbitrarily small collective energy scales} }finite microscopic energy scale+many states⇒arbitrarily small collective energy scales​

children.value: This gives us one meaning of emergence:
A large number of degrees of freedom can generate new physical scales and new low-energy phenomena that are absent in the microscopic constituents.

children.value: 13. More is different—but also sometimes simpler

children.label: 13. More is different—but also sometimes simpler

children.value: These two examples capture two fundamental aspects of condensed matter physics.
A large system can possess properties that none of its individual components possess:

children.html: new collective degrees of freedom and new energy scales.\boxed{ \text{new collective degrees of freedom and new energy scales}. }new collective degrees of freedom and new energy scales.​

children.value: A large system can become insensitive to most microscopic details:

children.html: different microscopic systems can obey the same macroscopic theory.\boxed{ \text{different microscopic systems can obey the same macroscopic theory}. }different microscopic systems can obey the same macroscopic theory.​
More is different.\boxed{ \text{More is different.} }More is different.​
More can also be simpler (universal).\boxed{ \text{More can also be simpler (universal).} }More can also be simpler (universal).​

children.value: This apparent paradox is one of the reasons condensed matter physics is simultaneously universal but diversified.
If every microscopic detail remained equally important at macroscopic scales, understanding a system containing
particles would be hopeless and not universal.
Instead, large systems often organize themselves into descriptions involving only a small number of collective variables and effective laws.
A macroscopic piece of matter might microscopically contain

children.value: 15. The central question of this course

children.label: 15. The central question of this course

children.value: The examples above suggest a general strategy.
Given a many-body system, we will repeatedly ask:
What are the microscopic degrees of freedom?
What happens as the number of degrees of freedom becomes large?
What new collective degrees of freedom appear?
What new energy or length scales emerge?
Is there a simpler effective description?
These questions are more fundamental than simply diagonalizing a Hamiltonian.
They form the conceptual foundation of condensed matter theory.
One way to think about condensed matter theory is through a hierarchy:

children.html: microscopic constituents\boxed{ \text{microscopic constituents} }microscopic constituents​
⇓\Downarrow⇓
many-body organization\boxed{ \text{many-body organization} }many-body organization​
⇓\Downarrow⇓
collective degrees of freedom\boxed{ \text{collective degrees of freedom} }collective degrees of freedom​
⇓\Downarrow⇓
effective theory\boxed{ \text{effective theory} }effective theory​
⇓\Downarrow⇓
universal macroscopic behavior.\boxed{ \text{universal macroscopic behavior}. }universal macroscopic behavior.​

children.value: Much of this course will consist of learning how to move between these levels.
In the next lectures, we will begin developing the language needed to describe quantum many-body systems efficiently.
Instead of labeling every particle individually, we will introduce occupation-number states and creation and annihilation operators.
The motivation should now be clear.
The problem is not simply that there are many particles.
The important point is that in many-body physics, the relevant description is often not based on tracking individual particles at all.
Instead, we want a language adapted to

children.html: collective states, occupations, and excitations.\boxed{ \text{collective states, occupations, and excitations}. }collective states, occupations, and excitations.​

children.value: Second quantization will provide precisely such a language.
